summary:
Peru does not criminalise consensual same-sex sexual activity, lawful since the 1924 Penal Code; the 1863 code had criminalised sodomy with penalties comparable to rape. The age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation under a 2012 Constitutional Court decision, and applies to trans and cisgender youth alike. Trans identity itself is not an offence.

Legal protection against discrimination and hate crime on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is absent. Government Decree Nº 1323 criminalised such discrimination with effect from 7 January 2017 through Articles 46 and 323 of the Penal Code; Congress voted 66–29 in May 2017 to strip those provisions, President Kuczynski's veto stood at that point, and the protections were subsequently removed as the Penal Code was reworked. Peru is one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage. The repeal was carried by Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members arguing the President lacked authority to issue the decree, following an April Constitutional Committee vote and a petition carrying one million signatures.

Access to public facilities matching gender identity is restricted by law. Law 32331, enacted 13 May 2025, bars trans people from using public restrooms according to their gender identity, a state-imposed limit on daily movement that can intensify hostile interactions in transit spaces. The underlying bills, 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR, presented by legislators including Jorge Montoya and Muñante of Honor y Democracia, also ban inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'; the committee approved the dictamen unanimously for plenary on 20 February 2025. The IDEHPUCP human-rights institute of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru finds the restriction openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their identity, implicitly casting trans people as harassment risks, and it invokes Inter-American Court of Human Rights Advisory Opinion OC-24/17, under which gender identity falls within protected personal autonomy and states must guarantee trans people's full rights. The institute also records dehumanising comparisons made by congressman Lizarzaburu on the floor.

The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents extends the restriction. Human Rights Watch reports that it mandates public-restroom entry be determined by 'biological sex', which bars trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their identity; that its vaguely worded child-protection articles, notably Article 4 on media and advertising and Article 5, enable censorship of identity-related, artistic and educational content; and that the minimum sentence for obscenity rose from three to four years. Human Rights Watch characterises child protection as a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

Violence against trans people is rising and recorded figures understate it. A July 2024 report finds hate crimes increasing in Peru with trans women most affected, and co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans human-rights defender and journalist, states that the recorded numbers are only a sub-registry. A 2012 Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia study found that 70% of trans women in Lima and Callao work in sex work, a documented exposure factor for police and public violence.

The torture and rape of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, ended in conviction on 15 December 2025: police officers Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León received 17 years' imprisonment, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It is Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Legal recognition of gender is partially available. Transgender Peruvians may change their legal name to match their gender identity. In 2014 the Constitutional Court barred gender-marker changes on national identity documents, then reversed itself in a ruling of 21 October 2016 published 8 November, permitting gender change through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law covering legal gender change without surgery and access to passports and other identity documents matching gender identity was introduced on 4 November 2016 and remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021.

Healthcare classifications have shifted in both directions. In May 2024 the government decreed 'transsexualism' a mental health problem in order to cover trans healthcare; after protests, MINSA revised the term to 'gender discordance' in June 2024 for health-insurance classification purposes, and in June 2024 health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described by Human Rights Watch as a step toward dignity for trans patients. Conversion therapy is banned in Peru for medical professionals, and in May 2024 MINSA reiterated that sexual orientation and gender identity are not diseases, a protection with direct bearing on trans and LGBTQ minors exposed to such practices.

Hostility is also institutional. Outright International reports that public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination; in July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, struck an anti-equality decree as unconstitutional; and an April 2025 law on foreign funding of NGOs lets authorities revoke registrations on 'public order and security' grounds, which risks being weaponised against queer organising. In April 2025 the television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed the first openly-lesbian congresswoman, Susel Paredes, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.
tangentialFactors:
Peru's gap in anti-discrimination coverage places it alongside only Paraguay and Guyana in South America, a regional outlier status that shapes what protection a trans visitor can expect from national law compared with neighbouring jurisdictions.

The advisory opinion of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights in OC-24/17, and the Rojas Marín judgment reached through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, give trans claimants a regional enforcement route that domestic legislation does not provide.

Public opinion is generationally split: 18–24-year-olds showed markedly more favourable attitudes toward homosexual people (66%) than the population overall (49%), and approval of same-sex marriage, 8.3% nationally in 2010, was higher among younger respondents. Pride marches have been held annually since 2002, with the oldest recorded march in 1984, indicating an established visible community presence alongside the legislative hostility.
localsOnly:
Trans Peruvians can change their legal name to match their gender identity, and since the Constitutional Court's ruling of 21 October 2016, published 8 November of that year, gender markers on national identity documents may be changed through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery.

The 2016 national education curriculum includes information on sexual orientation, sex and gender, describing sexual orientation as the product of complex biological, cognitive and environmental circumstances and not a voluntary choice.

Conversion therapy is prohibited for medical professionals, and MINSA stated in May 2024 that sexual orientation and gender identity are not diseases; the health ministry reclassified the insurance diagnosis from 'transsexualism' to 'gender discordance' in June 2024 and removed pathologising terminology from official guidance the same month.

Community organising faces added pressure: an April 2025 law on foreign funding allows NGO registration to be revoked on public-order grounds, congressional pressure continues against therapeutic abortion at the Instituto Materno Perinatal, and reported demands include a stable supply of HIV medication, the replacement of outdated medical rules, recognition of diverse families, equal marriage, and LGBTIQ+ quotas in public office.
outOfScopeNotes:
The status of the Gender Identity Law introduced on 4 November 2016 is unresolved beyond March 2021; no source in this inventory confirms whether it has since been enacted, withdrawn or remains pending.

Whether Law 32331 of 13 May 2025 and the April 2025 sexual-integrity law have been challenged or suspended in court is unresolved here; the only litigation recorded is the July 2025 Lima constitutional court ruling against a separate anti-equality decree.

Whether Decree Nº 1323's Articles 46 and 323 were reinstated in any later Penal Code reform is not sourced; the inventory documents their removal and the resulting absence of coverage, not any subsequent restoration.

Hate-crime counts are drawn from a report whose authors state the figures are only a sub-registry, so no reliable national total or conviction rate for anti-trans violence is available from these sources.
